o: It permanently updates the model weights with domain knowledge
It looks up cached answers from earlier sessions so repeated prompts skip the model
It retrieves related information from an external source and passes it to the model
It screens generated responses for harmful or restricted content
fixes.x: Which statement best describes what a RAG pipeline adds to a foundation model?
fixes.e: RAG fetches relevant content from an external knowledge source at inference time and injects it into the model's input; the weights are never touched. Looking up cached answers to repeated prompts describes response caching, which reuses old output instead of grounding a new one, and permanently updating weights describes fine-tuning.

o: A lightweight model on provisioned throughput with a one-year term
A lightweight model customized through a fine-tuning job
A lightweight model billed per token on demand
A lightweight model hosted on a dedicated always-on endpoint
fixes.e: A few dozen requests a day is the ideal case for pay-per-token on-demand pricing, since the nonprofit pays only for what it actually uses. Provisioned throughput with a term commitment and a dedicated always-on endpoint both bill for reserved capacity around the clock and only pay off at sustained high volume, while fine-tuning adds training and hosting costs this workload does not need.

o: A real-time endpoint that responds per request
An asynchronous endpoint that delivers results to a storage bucket
A serverless endpoint that scales to zero between requests
A batch transform job triggered whenever new records arrive
fixes.e: A persistent real-time endpoint keeps the model loaded and answers each call synchronously, the only pattern that reliably meets a sub-second bedside target. A serverless endpoint that scales to zero adds cold-start delays of several seconds, and asynchronous inference queues the request and drops the result in storage later instead of returning it to the waiting clinician.

o: Transcribing digitized audio interviews into text
Writing a caption for a supplied photograph
Retouching damaged photos by regenerating missing pixels
Retrieving newly published web articles on its own
Answering a question about a chart image
fixes.x: A publisher's archive team is evaluating a multimodal foundation model that accepts text and images as input and generates text. Which of these archive tasks does it fit? (Select TWO.)
fixes.e: A text-and-image multimodal model can examine a supplied photograph or chart and generate language about it, so captioning and visual question answering both fit. Transcribing audio requires a speech input modality the model does not accept, regenerating pixels requires image output it does not produce, and a foundation model cannot fetch new web content on its own without an external retrieval tool.

o: Provisioned Throughput
Batch inference
Compute Savings Plans
On-Demand invocation
fixes.x: A steady, high-volume assistant runs around the clock on Amazon Bedrock, and the team wants committed-term pricing with a guaranteed sustained request rate and no throttling. Which purchasing option fits?
fixes.e: Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model capacity for a committed term, locking in both price and a sustained request rate for predictable round-the-clock traffic. On-Demand carries no commitment and can be throttled at high volume, Batch inference discounts non-interactive jobs by trading away latency, and Compute Savings Plans do not cover Bedrock model invocation.

o: Lower the temperature setting to zero
Trim unnecessary text out of each prompt
Reduce the top-p sampling value
Decrease the number of retry attempts per request
Cap the maximum number of output tokens
fixes.e: Billing follows tokens in and tokens out, so trimming prompt text and capping the response length both shrink the bill directly. Lowering the temperature or the top-p value only changes how each next token is chosen, not how many tokens are billed, and retry settings matter only for failed calls, which generate no billable output to save on.

o: Levenshtein edit distance
Jaccard overlap of shared keywords
Cosine similarity
Term frequency counts
fixes.e: Cosine similarity compares the angle between embedding vectors, capturing closeness of meaning independent of magnitude, and it is the standard ranking metric in vector stores. Levenshtein edit distance counts character-level changes between raw strings rather than comparing embeddings, while Jaccard overlap and term frequency counts are keyword statistics, not vector comparisons.

o: The number of results returned for each query
The denied topics list in the guardrail
The stop sequence list used by the model
The schedule frequency of the sync job
fixes.x: A retrieval-augmented assistant produces well-formed answers that end cleanly yet omit supporting details reviewers confirm exist in the knowledge base, and last night's index sync completed without errors. Which retrieval setting should the team change?
fixes.e: When too few passages come back per query, relevant material never reaches the model's context, so answers sound complete but stay thin; raising the result count widens the evidence supplied. A denied-topics guardrail would block or deflect whole subjects rather than trim details, stop sequences would cut answers off mid-stream instead of letting them end cleanly, and a sync job that finished without errors has already placed the content in the index.

o: Regional availability and licensing terms
Inference speed and context window size
Supported languages and modality coverage
Parameter count and training data size
fixes.x: A regulated brokerage is choosing a foundation model. Data-residency rules require every inference call to run inside a specific geography, and counsel must sign off on how the provider permits commercial use before launch. Which criteria dominate the choice?
fixes.e: Compliance constraints filter the field before capability comparisons matter: a model not offered where the data must stay, or whose usage terms counsel rejects, is disqualified outright. Inference speed, context window size, language coverage, and parameter count are worth weighing only among the models that survive that eligibility screen.

o: Bias from label smoothing applied during model training
Bias caused by class imbalance across the labeled categories
Bias introduced by the human annotators during labeling
Bias arising from label leakage between the training and test splits
fixes.x: An annotation vendor based in a single country labeled every image in a wildlife-classification dataset. Reviewers later find many species tagged according to that country's local naming conventions rather than the agreed taxonomy. Which flaw entered the pipeline?
fixes.e: The ground truth itself reflects the conventions of one group of human labelers, so the model would learn those conventions as if they were fact, which is annotator-introduced bias. Label smoothing is a deliberate training-time regularization rather than a data flaw, and class imbalance or leakage between splits would distort proportions or evaluation without explaining why individual tags follow one country's naming habits.

o: Lowering the temperature toward zero
Expanding the maximum context window
Switching to an embeddings model for generation
Raising the temperature setting
fixes.e: Raising the temperature flattens the token probability distribution so lower-probability words are sampled more often, which makes the output more varied. Lowering it toward zero does the opposite and produces nearly deterministic text, and a larger context window changes how much input fits, not how diverse the output is.

o: The flagship model with response streaming enabled
The provider's smallest, lowest-cost model tier
A multimodal model that can interpret product photos
A fine-tuned copy of the flagship model with response caching
fixes.e: Type-ahead suggestions are a latency- and volume-dominated workload, so the provider's smallest, lowest-cost tier is the right fit when deep quality is not required. Streaming the flagship model improves perceived responsiveness but keeps the big model's slower time to first token and much higher per-request cost, and response caching only pays off when identical prompts repeat.

o: Each prediction follows an explicit rule path that can be read directly
Tree models generalize better on clinical data than neural networks
It attaches a calibrated confidence score to every risk level
It returns identical outputs for identical inputs, unlike a neural network
fixes.x: Hospital auditors must be able to justify every triage recommendation after the fact. A neural network scores slightly higher offline than a decision-tree alternative. Why might the team still choose the tree?
fixes.e: A decision tree is inherently interpretable: every prediction follows an explicit rule path that an auditor can read and defend directly, which can be worth a small offline accuracy gap in a regulated setting. A confidence score reports how sure the model is, not why it decided, and determinism is no differentiator because a trained neural network also returns identical outputs for identical inputs.

o: Failure patterns can be learned without any labeled examples of past failures
A model trained once will hold its accuracy without ongoing retraining
A model can pinpoint the physical root cause of each predicted failure
The failure signatures are too complex and numerous to write out as explicit rules
fixes.x: An airline wants to predict which spare parts will fail soon using years of accumulated sensor readings. What makes this problem a good candidate for machine learning rather than a hand-coded rules program?
fixes.e: Machine learning earns its keep when the relationships are too subtle and numerous for anyone to encode as explicit rules, which is exactly the case for failure signatures buried in years of sensor data. The other claims misstate what ML offers: supervised failure prediction still needs labeled failure history, accuracy drifts without retraining, and models surface correlated risk rather than pinpointing physical root causes.

o: Provisioned Throughput purchased with no commitment
Batch inference submitted as a single job
On-demand invocation for each individual record
Provisioned Throughput with a six-month commitment
fixes.x: A logistics company generates 400,000 shipment descriptions from a file exported every night, and the output is not needed until the following morning. Which Amazon Bedrock invocation mode keeps the cost of this workload lowest?
fixes.e: Batch inference processes large record sets asynchronously and is priced below the standard per-token rate, which fits work that can wait until morning. On-demand invocation for each individual record pays the full per-token price, and Provisioned Throughput in either form bills hourly for reserved capacity that would sit idle outside the nightly window.
